title: Events
summary: Event handler props, passing functions instead of calling them, the synthetic event object, propagation and default behaviour, and naming handler props.

sections.title: Pass a function, do not call it
sections.body: `onClick={handleClick}` passes the function. `onClick={handleClick()}` **calls it during render** and passes its return value, which usually means it fires on every render, and if it sets state it loops. To pass arguments, wrap it: `onClick={() => remove(id)}`.
sections.code:
<button onClick={save}>Save</button>             // right
<button onClick={() => remove(item.id)}>×</button> // right, with an argument
<button onClick={save()}>Save</button>           // wrong: runs while rendering

sections.title: The event object
sections.body:
Handlers receive a React event that wraps the native one with the same interface: `e.target`, `e.currentTarget`, `e.preventDefault()`, `e.stopPropagation()`; the native event is `e.nativeEvent`. `e.target` is where the event started; `e.currentTarget` is the element whose handler is running.

React attaches listeners at the root and simulates bubbling through your component tree, so events also bubble through **portals** to their React parents. `onScroll` is the exception: it does not bubble.

sections.title: Propagation and defaults
sections.body:
Events bubble from the target up through ancestors. Call `e.stopPropagation()` to stop parent handlers from running. Use `onClickCapture` to run a handler on the way down, before children.

`e.preventDefault()` stops browser behaviour such as a form submit reloading the page or a link navigating. It is separate from propagation: preventing the default does not stop bubbling, and stopping bubbling does not prevent the default.

sections.title: Naming and owning handlers
sections.body:
By convention, handler **props** are named `onSomething` (`onSelect`, `onClose`) and the functions you write are named `handleSomething`. The component that owns the state defines the handler and passes it down; children just call `onSelect(id)`.

Event handlers are the main place for side effects, because they run in response to a user action and not during rendering. Unlike rendering code, they do not need to be pure.

pitfalls: Using `e.target` when you meant the element with the handler (`e.currentTarget`).
Forgetting `preventDefault()` on form submit and getting a full page reload.
Assuming `stopPropagation` also prevents the default action.

gotchas.question: What logs when the button is clicked?
gotchas.answer: "button" then "div". The click bubbles from the button to the div.

gotchas.question: What logs when the button is clicked?
gotchas.code: console.log("capture")} onClick={() => console.log("div")}>
gotchas.answer: "capture" then "button". Capture handlers run first on the way down; `stopPropagation` then stops the bubble before it reaches the div's `onClick`.
